answers_by_date.basis: Ley 22.439 (1981) was in force. Its only asylum provision, art. 25 on territorial asylum granted by the Interior Ministry, sets no duty to tell a person facing rejection or expulsion (arts. 37-39) that asylum may be available. No practice evidence was needed because there was no protection.
Ley 25.871 had been in force since 21 Jan 2004. Its border-rejection rule (art. 35) and expulsion rules (arts. 61-62) contain no duty to inform about asylum. Ley 26.165 did not yet exist.

Ley 26.165 (Dec 2006), art. 39, makes any official who learns that a foreigner wants to seek refugee status responsible for non-refoulement and for notifying the Executive Secretariat. That is a duty triggered by the person's own request, not a duty to tell them asylum exists. Arts. 2 and 7 ban rejection at the border and refoulement but impose no duty to inform.

Decreto 616/2010 (in force July 2010), art. 35(a), only says that refugee obligations under arts. 39-40 of Ley 26.165 must be observed at border rejection. It creates no duty to inform. No change through 2020, DNU 70/2017 included.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

answers.repealed_search: I read Ley 22.439 (the asylum chapter, art. 25, and expulsion arts. 37-39), the original Ley 25.871, Ley 26.165, Decreto 616/2010 and DNU 70/2017. None of them required informing people about asylum before rejection or expulsion. I found no repealed or narrowed protection. Decreto 1023/94 and the CEPARE rules (Decreto 464/85) were not read.
answers.sourcing_note: Original texts read on InfoLEG and argentina.gob.ar. Ley 22.439 was read as displayed on argentina.gob.ar; I only saw the first page of its list of amending norms.
answers.notes: No treaty provision was relied on.

answers_by_date.basis: Ley 22.439, art. 37, allowed expulsion 'to the country of origin, nationality, provenance, or another that would admit him', with no bar on chain refoulement. Refugees had only the 1951 Convention (art. 33) and CEPARE decrees, which do not expressly bar onward refoulement.
Ley 25.871 (2004) has no rule on the destination of expulsions that bars onward refoulement. Ley 26.165 did not yet exist.

Ley 26.165, art. 8 (in force since Dec 2006), lets an expelled refugee be sent only to a State that guarantees protection against expulsion, return or extradition. This covers refugees only, not migrants generally. The starting answer is kept: no event between 2006 and 2020 changed art. 8 (see concern).
Same as 2010. Art. 8 of Ley 26.165 is unchanged; neither Decreto 616/2010 nor, later, DNU 70/2017 touched it.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been no right protections neither in 2000 nor in 2020

answers.repealed_search: I read Ley 22.439 art. 37 (expulsion to 'otro que lo admitiera', with no safeguard), the original Ley 25.871 and DNU 70/2017. None barred chain refoulement for migrants generally. The only protection found, Ley 26.165 art. 8 (refugees), was added in 2006 and never repealed.
answers.sourcing_note: Ley 26.165 was read in its original text; InfoLEG shows no amendment to art. 8. Ley 22.439 was read on argentina.gob.ar.
answers.starting_answer_concern: For 2023 the MRD coded 'Yes', citing Ley 26.165 art. 8. That text has been in force unchanged since December 2006. If art. 8 is enough for 'Yes' (refugees only), the 2020 'No' is inconsistent, and 'Yes' would hold from 2010 onward. If refugee-only coverage is not enough, then the 2023 'Yes' is the inconsistent one. No event between 2020 and 2023 explains the difference.
answers.notes: The 1951 Refugee Convention (approved by Ley 15.869) was not treated as giving an express chain-refoulement bar.

answers_by_date.basis: Ley 22.439: expulsion only by the migration authority or Interior Ministry on statutory grounds (arts. 37, 38, 95), 'al constatar la ilegalidad'. But art. 39 allowed immediate expulsion of clandestine entrants 'ante la sola constatación del hecho', and there was no judicial review (art. 80). Practice evidence is thin and second-hand: in the De la Torre case (IACHR Report 85/11, read only through search results) a resident was arrested without a warrant and expelled within a week in 1996.

Ley 25.871 had been in force since 21 Jan 2004. Expulsion must follow a summons to regularise that weighs personal circumstances, with automatic judicial review (art. 61), on grounds in art. 62. Art. 66 requires each case to be 'examinado y decidido individualmente'. The law was not yet regulated, and no practice source for 2005 could be read (the CELS 2005 PDF would not open).

Same provisions; Decreto 616/2010 was not yet in force. The CMW (2011) found that the DNM did not weigh personal and family circumstances when ordering expulsions on art. 29 impediments, but it acknowledged the safeguards, including automatic judicial review.

Ley 25.871 arts. 61, 62, 66, 74, 89, now with Decreto 616/2010 (in force July 2010), whose art. 61 requires written, understandable notice and up to 30 days to regularise. No later practice source for about 2015 was read; the rating relies on CMW 2011 and lowers confidence.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but they are not the same

answers.sourcing_note: Ley 22.439, the original Ley 25.871, Decreto 616/2010 and DNU 70/2017 were all read. Practice evidence for 2000 and 2005 is thin: the CELS 2000-2005 PDFs and the IACHR De la Torre report could not be opened, so those ratings are low-confidence.
answers.notes: I coded 'Yes' in 2000 because Ley 22.439 made expulsion an administrative act on statutory grounds. A stricter reader might say 'No', given art. 39's summary expulsion and the absence of judicial review.

answers_by_date.basis: Ley 22.439, arts. 73-82: a request for reconsideration or revocation within 10 working days, and an appeal to the Interior Ministry against expulsion (art. 78(b)) that suspends it (art. 82). But the Ministry's decision was final with no further remedy (art. 80), and art. 39 summary expulsions bypassed review. Practice evidence is thin and second-hand (De la Torre, 1996, through search results).

Ley 25.871 (since 21 Jan 2004): administrative and judicial review of expulsion orders (arts. 74-84), suspensive effect (art. 82), free legal aid and interpreters (art. 86), judicial review of legality and reasonableness (art. 89). The law was unregulated and no 2005 practice source could be read.
Same provisions. The CMW (2011) noted automatic judicial review, rights of appeal and free legal aid, while criticising gaps in DNM practice.
The same Ley 25.871 provisions, now regulated by Decreto 616/2010. No later practice source was read; the rating extrapolates from CMW 2011.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 but they are not the same
